paragraphs.source_en: I listened quietly, in turn, to the stories told by the three men, and found them neither funny nor sad. It seemed to me that human beings, merely to pass the time, force their mouths into motion, laughing over things that are not funny and making much of things that are not very interesting; beyond that, they have no particular talent at all. I had long known that my master was narrow-minded and willful. But since he was not usually much given to speech, I felt there was something about him that was somewhat hard to grasp. That very quality had even made him seem a little frightening to me. Yet after hearing what he had just said, I suddenly felt rather inclined to despise him. Why could he not keep silent and listen honestly to what the other two had to say? What could he possibly gain by refusing to be outdone and spouting such utterly pointless nonsense? Could Epictetus have written in his Discourses that one ought to behave in such a fashion? In short, my master, Kangetsu, and Meitei alike are idle gentlemen of a peaceful age; like gourds swaying on the vine in the wind, they seem to imagine themselves detached from the world, but in fact they have not forgotten the dust of this life and are full of worldly feeling. The spirit of rivalry, the urge to prevail over others, shows itself now and then even in their ordinary jokes and conversation. If they sink any further, they will become creatures of the same hole as the vulgar people they are always denouncing. Seen from the standpoint of us cats, that is truly pitiful. The only difference is that their speech and behavior, unlike those of the usual half-baked know-it-alls, do not carry that tiresome set pattern; in that respect there is at least something to be said for them.

paragraphs.source_en: Thinking this, I suddenly lost interest in the three men’s conversation and decided I might as well go see Miss Tortoiseshell. So I made my way to the garden entrance of the lady teacher of the two-stringed koto. Looking in, I saw that the New Year pine decorations and sacred ropes had already been taken down, and though ten days had passed since the New Year, the bright spring sun shone over all beneath a cloudless blue sky, making the little garden of less than ten tsubo seem even livelier than it had under the dawn light of New Year’s Day. On the veranda there was only a single cushion; no one was in sight, the sliding doors were shut tight, and the lady teacher had probably gone to the bathhouse. Whether the teacher was home or not was naturally of no concern; what worried me was whether Miss Tortoiseshell’s health had improved at all. All around was quiet, with no sign of anyone at home, so I climbed onto the veranda with mud on all four paws, lay down in the middle of the cushion, and found it wonderfully comfortable. Growing drowsy, I forgot all about Miss Tortoiseshell and without noticing it slipped into a doze. Just then, a human voice suddenly came from inside the sliding doors:
